note: ep07 v2 'The Nguyens: 15 or 30?' (2026-10-23). First episode of the proposed family series: Minh and Lan buy their first house in 2026; Uncle Tu took a 15-year loan in January 1993; the replay runs two versions of Tu on the pinned FRED + Shiller data (the 1993-01 cohort is the median of the 58 completed windows). Every spoken number is checked by tools/validate-ep07-story.mjs. Replay lines carry `year` (years since signing). Speakers: N narrator, M Minh, L Lan, T Uncle Tu (kitchen), A Tu who took the 15 (left panel), B Tu who took the 30 (right panel). `*word*` = emphasis. The family are illustrations.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Minh and Lan are buying their first house in America. A *four hundred thousand dollar* loan. And the bank gives them a choice.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Fifteen years, at six and a half percent: about *thirty-five hundred* a month. Or thirty years, at seven percent: about *twenty-seven hundred* a month.

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: Fifteen. I don't want to owe the bank for thirty years.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: But with the thirty, we pay *eight hundred less* every month. We could invest that.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: Listen to Lan. I took the fifteen in nineteen ninety-three. *Best thing I ever did.*

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Maybe. But what if you had taken the thirty, and invested the difference?

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Good question. And we can actually check. Same house, same month, January nineteen ninety-three. Same cash every month. *Two versions of Uncle Tu.*

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the left, what he really did: the fifteen. On the right, the thirty, investing the difference every single month. The red bar is what he still owes. The green bag is what he has invested.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Two thousand. Stocks are booming. I've already got *sixty-four thousand* invested.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Nothing invested yet. Every dollar goes to the house. But I owe less every month.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Two thousand three. The dot-com crash. My savings fell to *forty-eight thousand*.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Two thousand eight. My house is *paid off*! Now I invest the whole payment, every month.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And he starts right as the two thousand eight crash hits. *Buying stocks on sale.* The other Tu takes his second crash.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Twenty twenty-three. Thirty years. *Four hundred eighteen thousand* invested. No mortgage.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: My house is paid off too. *Three hundred twenty-eight thousand.*

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So Uncle Tu was right, by about *ninety thousand dollars*, in nineteen ninety-three money. And not because stocks did badly. They grew almost ten percent a year. The thirty's savings were simply biggest right when *two crashes* hit.

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: So I'm right. The fifteen always wins.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Not so fast. We ran every month you could have signed since nineteen ninety-one. Every loan old enough to finish, *fifty-eight* of them, was signed when rates were about seven to nine percent. The fifteen won *all fifty-eight*.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Later loans haven't finished yet, so check them at the halfway mark, year fifteen. Signed in the nineties, at high rates: the thirty was *never* ahead. Signed two thousand five to twenty eleven, at about four to seven percent: the thirty was ahead *every time*.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So it's not fifteen good, thirty bad. *The rate you sign at decides.*

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Then what about us, at seven percent?

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: At seven on the thirty and six and a half on the fifteen, the money you invest has to earn more than *eight percent a year*, every year, just to tie. And you have to invest it *every single month*, for thirty years.

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: Minh. You can't even keep a gym membership for three months.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Okay. Fair.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: But there's a third option. Take the thirty-year loan, and *pay it like a fifteen*. You're done eleven months later, and it costs about nine percent of the loan extra. In exchange, any month things go wrong, you can drop to the lower payment.

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: So we pay it off fast, like I want.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: And we keep a safety net. *Deal.*

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So what does this mean for you? *Lesson one.* The rate you sign at decides. When rates were high, the fifteen came out ahead. When they were low, the thirty was ahead at the halfway mark.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: *Lesson two.* At today's rates, the thirty only wins if you invest the difference every month, and it earns more than about eight percent a year.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: *Lesson three.* Can't decide? Take the thirty and pay it like a fifteen. You keep the option to slow down.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The fine print. Freddie Mac survey rates, from the month you sign. Stocks are the S and P with dividends, no fees. No refinancing, no taxes, no points. The thirty-year borrower never skips a month. The finished loans all come from one era, overlapping. The family are illustrations. The history is real. This is history, not advice.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Which would you pick: Lan's fifteen, Minh's thirty, or the deal they made? Tell me in the comments.
